extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent lawyers, empirical researchers, and policymakers interested in patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical measurement and statistical analysis of patent litigation outcomes (win rates, invalidity, infringement) broken down by technology area and industry, including regression controls and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitive win rate (patentee definitive winner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees overall won just 26 percent of cases that went to a definitive outcome. We included as patentee definitive wins only those cases that resulted in a judgment for the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts only definitive merits rulings (judgments). Excludes cases in which there was a summary judgment denial followed by a settlement before trial; note that different counting conventions (e.g., treating settlements with payment as patentee wins) will change industry/technology win rates (example: Holman's different counting increased biotech patentee wins). Report percentages by technology and industry and test statistical significance (Pearson χ2, p-values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity rate (all grounds, any stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: While roughly 43.0 percent of patents that went to a final judgment on validity were invalidated, the technology-specific numbers ranged from 21.4 percent for optics and 25.6 percent for chemistry to 80.0 percent for biotechnology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition invalidity percentages on a final determination of a validity dispute. Break down by technology and industry. Report frequency and percentage, and use chi-square tests to assess significance. Note that some cases have both invalidity and noninfringement findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement rate (direct infringement, literal plus DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent of cases that resolved an infringement dispute finding the patents to be infringed (literal plus doctrine of equivalents). Example: chemistry patents won infringement disputes more than two-thirds of the time (68.4%), software patents were found infringed in 19.7% of resolved infringement disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition infringement percentages on final determinations of infringement. Break down by technology and industry. Include sub-analysis separating business-method and non-business-method software patents (different infringement rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss classification: invalidity versus noninfringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When patentees lost, losses can be classified as loss on invalidity or loss on noninfringement. Across technologies, the chance of a patent being held not infringed was significantly higher than the chance of it being held invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts and percentages of each loss type by technology/industry. Note that some claims are held both invalid and not infringed, so percentages may not sum to 100. Use tables to show losses by type (e.g., Table 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment invalidity win rate (defendant SJ wins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are more likely to grant summary judgment of invalidity when confronted with biotechnology and software patents; e.g., 43.9% of adjudicated SJ motions on invalidity for business-method patents were granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report SJ outcomes separately from definitive merits rulings. Note that SJ wins are definitive for defendant purposes. Use chi-square tests for differences across technologies. Be cautious comparing SJ win rates to final-win rates because of differences in counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 102 prior-art invalidity success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Success rate on § 102 prior-art arguments varies by technology (example frequencies and percentages reported; overall 31.2% success in the sample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequency and percentage of § 102 wins by technology. Note the Pearson χ2 significance and condition on 'any stage' of proceedings. Mention that this table covers arguments in all procedural postures, not just SJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 103 obviousness invalidity success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Success rate on § 103 obviousness arguments varies by technology (reported frequencies and percentages; overall ~29.9% in the sample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequency and percentage by technology and across procedural postures. Use chi-square tests to assess significance of differences across technology categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 112(b) indefiniteness success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness arguments under § 112(b) show strong technology differences—never successful in mechanical or biotech in this sample, succeeded nearly one-quarter of the time in software patent cases and about one-third in electronics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report success rates by technology. Discuss doctrinal reasons (e.g., lack of standard language in software claims, means-plus-function issues) and cite relevant Federal Circuit cases (Aristocrat line).

rubrics_metrics.name: § 112 enablement/written description (inadequate disclosure) success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments based on enablement and written description (whether claim scope is supported by disclosure) show very different patterns: one-third of mechanical patent decisions and three-quarters of biotechnology patent decisions on these grounds resulted in invalidity, far more than in software and electronics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequency and percentage by technology. Note small sample caveats for technologies like biotechnology and potential loss of significance when adding full controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate software into business-method vs non-business-method
rubrics_metrics.description: When separating business-method and non-business-method patents, business-method patents fared substantially better than other software patents on some measures (e.g., patentee wins 17% for business-method vs 12% for non-business-method), but business-methods were more likely to be invalidated on certain grounds (e.g., §112 indefiniteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include separate categories in tables and regressions for software business-method and software non-business-method. Report differences in invalidity, infringement, and SJ grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rule for counting patentee 'wins' (treatment of settlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors counted as patentee definitive wins only those cases that resulted in a judgment for the patentee. Others (e.g., settlements with payments) were not counted as definitive wins for the patentee in the primary measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about how settlements, SJ denials followed by settlement, and monetary payments are treated. Differences in coding (counting settlements as wins) can materially affect statistics by technology/industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent and lawsuit characteristics as regression controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression models incorporate patent characteristics (domestic/foreign status of inventors, number of claims, prior art references cited, number of other patents that cite the patent) and lawsuit characteristics (patent age at filing, number of defendants sued, number of other patents asserted in the same case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these controls in multivariate regressions when testing technology/industry effects to reduce confounding. Report coefficients, p-values, and conduct F-tests for joint technology/industry effects. Note degrees-of-freedom constraints when including many district dummies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical robustness practices: clustering, bootstrapping, F-tests, and FDR caution
rubrics_metrics.description: To account for correlated observations, the authors simultaneously clustered standard errors on unique patent numbers and cases. They also performed bootstrap logistic regressions (1,000 draws) and reported F-tests for joint effects. They caution about the false discovery rate (FDR) when running multiple tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneously cluster on patent and case to handle interdependence. Use bootstrap sampling to improve standard error accuracy when distribution is unknown. Run F-tests to assess whether technology or industry 'matters' overall. Discuss FDR and avoid over-interpreting marginal p-values (particularly p < 0.10); report precise p-values in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-of-litigation sensitivity (trial vs summary judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology differences are not evident at trial or on summary judgment of noninfringement (not statistically significant), but there are significant differences in willingness of courts to grant summary judgment of invalidity across technologies (higher for biotech and software).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze outcomes separately by procedural posture (trial, summary judgment, other stages). Report and test whether technology effects differ by stage; interpret differences carefully (e.g., SJ invalidity grants may drive overall differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioning and sample definition notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity and invalidity decisions are conditioned on a final determination of a validity dispute. The authors also ran alternative specifications allowing patents secondary technology codes, increasing observations from 636 definitive merits outcomes to 777, with some effects on category-specific rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about conditioning (e.g., condition invalidity rates on adjudicated validity disputes). Consider alternative coding specifications (primary vs secondary technology classifications) and report sensitivity of results to those choices.
